title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.

title: Belief Cascades Drive Persuasion in LLM Agent Networks
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly debate answers, coordinate research, simulate users, and mediate information flows, making agent-to-agent persuasion a basic but undermeasured capability. We introduce a controlled testbed for studying how goal-directed persuaders shift elicited stances in networks of LLM agents grounded in real-world ego-network topologies. Across four LLM backbones, five graphs, and 55 policy statements, we find that persuasion dynamics depend on the interaction between topology, competition, topic, and model prior. Additionally, we show that direct exposure reliably predicts next-round stance change in competing runs, and peer relays carry smaller but measurable influence, showing that agents not assigned to persuade can still transmit persuasive force. Finally, analyzing post text alone misses important movement: planned strategies are only partly realized in executed messages, action choices can diverge from message content, and persuadees rarely state the stance shifts detected by probes. These results argue for evaluating multi-agent persuasion as a trajectory- and exposure-level process, using belief probes, exposure provenance, and action logs to identify who influenced whom and whether visible language reflects underlying stance movement.

title: SeeNav-Agent: Enhancing Vision-Language Navigation with Visual Prompt and Step-Level Policy Optimization
abstract: Existing Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) agents based on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often suffer from errors of perception, reasoning, and planning, which significantly hinder their navigation performance. To address these limitations, a novel VLN agent framework, named SeeNav-Agent, is proposed. First, to reduce hallucinations of the visual module of the VLN agent, a dual-view Visual Prompt (VP) technique is introduced, which can also improve the agent's understanding of current spatial states. Subsequently, a novel step-level Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) method, Step Reward Group Policy Optimization (SRGPO), is designed for post-training. In SRGPO, we first define verifiable process rewards for navigation, and then perform efficient step-level advantage estimation by randomly grouping navigation steps. SRGPO provides dense reward signals for the RFT of the VLN agent and enhances its planning capability. Experiments on both the EmbodiedBench Navigation (Embench-Nav) and VLN-CE validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. By introducing the zero-shot VP module, the GPT-4.1 achieves a navigation success rate of 86.7%, surpassing the current best LVLM by approximately 20 percentage points (pp) on Embench-Nav and achieves an 11.1 pp improvement on VLN-CE compared to the base model. With VP+SRGPO, the Qwen2.5-VL-3B model reaches a navigation success rate of 72.3%, outperforming the best existing LVLM model by 5.6 pp on Embench-Nav and achieves 8.9 pp improvement on VLN-CE compared to the baseline method. Moreover, compared to GRPO and GiGPO, the proposed SRGPO demonstrates significant improvements in training stability, convergence efficiency, and generalization capability.

title: Automating Formal Verification with Reinforcement Learning and Recursive Inference
abstract: Automated formal verification remains challenging for large language models because data for proof assistants and verification-aware languages is scarce, and correctness depends on satisfying precise machine-checkable specifications rather than producing plausible code. This thesis studies how verifier environments can improve LLM generation of verified programs and proofs through reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) and verifier-guided inference-time search. First, we train open-source models in Dafny with RLVR using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and related variants, assembling generated candidates into complete programs and scoring them with compiler and verifier outcomes. Initial experiments on an APPS-derived Dafny dataset increased verified reward from 2.2% to 58.1%, but revealed specification hacking, where models exploit weak formal specifications instead of implementing the intended solutions. After filtering underspecified and vulnerable tasks, multi-turn RLVR on the refined benchmark improves the verified pass rate from 9.7% to 31.1%. Second, we develop a verifier-guided inference scaffold in Lean that treats proof generation as structured search over decomposed subgoals, verifier feedback, diagnostics, and repair. With a fixed base model, the full scaffold with proof reviser improves pass rate on an initial VeriCoding pilot set from 46.2% under direct repair to 69.2%. On the larger VERINA dataset, whole-task decomposition plus proof reviser solves 7 of 42 previously unsolved tasks. We also introduce Dalek-Bench, a repository-scale Lean benchmark derived from the Rust $\texttt{curve25519-dalek}$ verification project; preliminary results remain weak, indicating that stronger progress evaluation and task-specific tool-use policies are still needed.

title: Can a Robot Become a Movie Director? Learning Artistic Principles for Aerial Cinematography
abstract: Aerial filming is constantly gaining importance due to the recent advances in drone technology. It invites many intriguing, unsolved problems at the intersection of aesthetical and scientific challenges. In this work, we propose a deep reinforcement learning agent which supervises motion planning of a filming drone by making desirable shot mode selections based on aesthetical values of video shots. Unlike most of the current state-of-the-art approaches that require explicit guidance by a human expert, our drone learns how to make favorable viewpoint selections by experience. We propose a learning scheme that exploits aesthetical features of retrospective shots in order to extract a desirable policy for better prospective shots. We train our agent in realistic AirSim simulations using both a hand-crafted reward function as well as reward from direct human input. We then deploy the same agent on a real DJI M210 drone in order to test the generalization capability of our approach to real world conditions. To evaluate the success of our approach in the end, we conduct a comprehensive user study in which participants rate the shot quality of our methods. Videos of the system in action can be seen at https://youtu.be/qmVw6mfyEmw.

title: Transitional Justice from the Margins: Intersections of Identities, Power and Human Rights
abstract: The call for papers for this special 10th anniversary issue was launched with high hopes and a commitment that voices from the margins would take up the invitation, not only to be heard, but to shape the Journal’s agenda in the coming years. This issue is positioned at the intersection of transitional justice, social repression and everyday lives. It reclaims and reaffirms the necessity of addressing marginality, vulnerability and exclusion, and engaging with the conditions that have produced systematic and sustained human rights violations in transitional societies. It also affirms the capacity of individuals and groups at the margins to exercise agency in everyday acts and ordinary but embedded resistance. As transitional justice has become part of mainstream thinking and an international patois that has emerged in response to atrocities and violent repression, the Journal has increasingly returned to foundational questions of knowledge production and justice practice in the field. This special issue opens a conversation that starts not from a series of normative assumptions about truth, justice and reparation but rather by paying attention to how transitional justice intersects with and may reinforce structural dimensions of marginalization in everyday lives. As a discourse based in the legal framework of international human rights law, transitional justice has been criticized for having an overly narrow, legalistic focus that elevates certain civil and political rights and fails to address other pervasive social and economic realities and dynamics.1 Systemic structural inequalities that may have precipitated civil protest and fuelled violent conflict in the first place, are often deprioritized and treated as policy matters to be dealt with ‘down the road.’ Economic and social justice conversations have been stymied, deemed insufficiently urgent or relevant to bring into the fulcrum of transitional justice bargaining. Crisis-driven governments, along with the international community, persistently turn their attention to the normative legal architecture and conceptual framework of peace agreements addressing (in theory) the immediate urgency of bringing armed conflict to an end. Such appeals sometimes echo the calls of high-profile local negotiators to focus on the violence at hand, not the systematic and institutional violence that underlies the resort to particularized violence in particularized circumstances. But, in this alignment, a hierarchy of issues frequently emerges reflecting the status quo power dynamics and priorities of the state and elites. Deep-rooted structural oppressions, essential conditions conducive to many gross violations of human rights, are set aside or assumed to be taken care of by finely crafted political commitments that are without either timeframes or targets. Here, human rights attention often centres on and may become shackled by failures to advance accountability for individual, high-profile violations, and high-profile violations to the body (torture, disappearances, extrajudicial execution, rape) dominate justice claims. We do not dismiss the urgency, pathos and harm created by these violations. However, they are intimately related to underpinning poverty, bedrock institutional beneficiaries and losers, sophisticated gerrymandering, colonial legacies and social and economic suprastructures. Meanwhile, the collective resistance of those most directly affected by social repressions and human rights violations is ignored or marginalized and makes little difference to mainstream transitional justice measures or to the states involved and their international partners. The transitional justice field continues to grapple with the challenges of power, elitism, exclusions, preference and privilege. As a field which was itself considered marginal,2 transitional justice has worked hard to prove its intellectual bona fides, its value to stakeholders and its usefulness as a set of ‘solutions’ to intractable governance and legal problems. In doing so, transitional justice has also produced its own set of elite actors and interests.3 There is often a certain cognitive dissonance in having elite transitional justice scholars and practitioners speaking to and about the experiences of those who have been the victims of harm in situations of repression and conflict from the comfortable distance of nonwar, nonrepression and often from the vantage point of the global North.4 We acknowledge this tension, mediated in part by our unique situation in Northern Ireland, a former conflict zone now transitional space located in a western democracy, sitting on the edge of Western Europe. As the cacophony of voices in this special issue attests, ‘who speaks for whom’ remains a deeply challenging question in the field of transitional justice. One thread running through all articles in this issue is the acknowledgement of discounted and disregarded voices, and a strong commitment through ethnographic research methods to redress the obvious imbalances, albeit in imperfect fashion. The mediation is always limited, and representation of the elusive realities of harm as experienced through intersectional identities always falls short, not only because of the incommensurability of violence, but due to the yawning gaps that exist between experience and observation. As the special issue attests, the modalities of transitional justice have both ‘top-down’ and ‘bottom-up’ features (e.g., UN gender policy versus local women’s committees), which exist in tension with one another. Critics of the field have concentrated on its lack of sustained ‘grassroots’ commitment and its failure (despite a self-defined commitment to victim-centredness) to deliver in practice.5 In our view, some of these critiques are overstated, and there is plenty of evidence of practical coalitions and partnerships between grassroots and elite actors in the field. Moreover, the assumptions that grassroots actors do not use elite strategies and are unsophisticated in their navigation of transitional justice praxis do a disservice to the erudition of victims and their representatives. Knowledge in transitional justice has always gone ‘both ways,’ bottom-up and top-down, and the building blocks of the field are a unique mix of the expected and unexpected. Even as we expose the fault lines of insiders and outsiders, we should pay critical attention to the ways in which those assumed to be powerless exercise agency, resistance and defiance and be simultaneously aware that power is exercised, with vulnerability and invincibility, and its strength is sometimes in the eye of the beholder only. Yet, that acknowledgement of the locations of capacity, insight, knowledge and strategy goes hand in hand with the ongoing realities of power and exclusion. Despite the gains made by marginalized groups, including indigenous, economic and socially excluded persons, youth, women, minorities, LGBTQI+ (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex) persons, there are insidious gaps in what we know of the experience of certain others, how they are heard, and the patterns of knowledge production and sharing that exclude them. Moreover, transitional justice settlements benefit some more than others, and there are distinct patterns to who is privileged and who is left out. Marginality, however constructed, is often not compressed to a single category (e.g., women) but rather consistently intersects with other socially excluded experiences (social and economic disadvantage, race, ethnicity, sexual orientation). This special issue seeks to pry open these intersectionalities, exclusions and beneficiaries. We aimed from the outset to expose the circulations of multilayered systemic power at the intersections of gender–race–class–age, and/or sexualities within diverse geographies–jurisdictions. Some have suggested that, at best, the narrow gender lens of transitional justice has fixated on women’s individualized gender-based experience of sexual violation at the cost of ignoring the power and identity dynamics that underpin, mandate and authorize violations in the first place. This focus on individualized violent incidents can be a form of ‘othering’ that decontextualizes social oppression, renders institutional racism invisible and fosters a wilful blindness to (intended and unintended) racist discourse within transitional justice. In a forthright appraisal, Canadian scholar Sherene Razack characterizes this as a form of ‘stealing the pain of others.’6 This special issue has a number of contributions that contend with the properties of group membership and its connection to victim status. Other contributions are painfully aware of the commodification of victims, their stories, pain and misfortune and the fundamental contradiction in the reality that the field of transitional justice sometimes needs victims more than victims need transitional justice. Victims are increasingly aware of this framing of their suffering and struggle to make sense of it, and are sometimes able to reposition their own strengths in the light of it. Women’s experiences of harm mediated through intersectional identities are prominently addressed in this issue. In an article written over 10 years ago, we first called for greater attention to intersectionality in transitional justice theory and practice. The articles in this issue affirm that the need for intersectional analysis has never been more pressing and more relevant. Kimberlé Crenshaw has examined how an exclusive focus on women as individual victims of a singular injustice may lead to a racialized revictimization within a legal system that seamlessly reproduces patriarchal and racialized power in the very moment that it affords recognition to gender oppression.7 Her work – and that of other intersectional scholars writing ‘from the margins’ – documents the role of structural oppression in constituting the conditions of lived experience that constrain minoritized and marginalized communities and their struggles for justice. Their analyses seek to expose and explain how masculinized identity discourses, which are shaped by colonization, invasion and historical intersections of race, class and gender oppressions, produce a dehumanized ‘other’ that justifies economic exploitation and extraordinary brutality. Intersectional gendered oppression in marginalized women’s lives is the central site of analysis in this special issue. This critical scholarship provides an intersectional framework for generating different forms of social justice work and energizing transformational change. Those acting and writing ‘from the margins’ or constructing knowledge from ‘the bottom up’ challenge others in the transitional justice field to interrogate the present dominant frameworks for the lives they ignore, the injustices they fail to see and the patriarchal and racialized power structures that remain intact and unexamined. As feminist scholars, we continue to demand intersectional analysis, and encourage the increasingly large and self-identified group of feminists writing within the transitional justice field to pay attention to class, socioeconomic status, disability, age and sexual orientation in gendering transition. We do a disservice to gender justice when these essential matters are simply ignored and deemed irrelevant to theoretical approaches and policy solutions. A number of contributors to this special issue discuss the limits of transitional justice as a framework for understanding the causes and redressing the collective effects of gross violations of human rights. They introduce new thinking, novel theorizations and action-driven research methods that inform scholarship with activist insights grounded in promoting grassroots knowledge. These contributions call critical attention to marginalized lives. They speak urgently of issues that really matter to an increasingly diverse and complex global community that often appears to be otherwise occupied. The articles fall into a number of overlapping and related categories. Historical and philosophical reflection is found in the article by C.K. Martin Chung, ‘Against Loveless Judging: Fritz Bauer and Transitional Justice in Postwar Germany.’ Based on the writings of Fritz Bauer, who was a central actor in the postwar West German transition, the article draws attention to his concept of judging a painful era ‘with love,’ including compassion, public education and repair as a form of ethical, methodological and substantive contract with the ‘loveless judging’ of the Nazi era. The freshness of new ideas and methodologies to the reimagining of transitional justice gives us new tools and ways of thinking to advance new work. The ethical introspection and cross-cutting ethical approaches advocated by this article allow us to conceive of intersectionality as a form of methodological shift, encompassing not only feminist theory but broadly applicable to philosophical and moral reasoning in the transitional justice space. Thus, shifting accepted wisdom in relation to the complex questions of punishment, resistance, reparation and cultural resocialization enhances not only vocabulary but also positionality. We remake the world with words, we reprioritize with new knowledge, and we undo what we know when it is replaced or substituted/enlightened with new awareness. In this realm, the role of memory and remembering is critical. Sylvanna Falcón’s article, ‘Intersectionality and the Arts: Counterpublic Memory-Making in Post-Conflict Peru,’ calls our attention to alternative sites of knowledge production led by (outsider) nonstate actors. These projects capture how art and display can visualize and restructure the public sphere, such that they constitute new tensions needling at hegemonic disputes about truth and harm. The author’s analysis of three public, feminist-led art projects in Peru illuminates the legacies of marginalization that have been conveniently forgotten by urban and state elites. Here transitional justice theory intersects with transitional justice as a cultural discourse that destabilizes the state in highly subversive ways. Ethnographic methodology brings the subaltern voices of those who survived widespread structural and systemic violence to the fore, underscoring how gender, race/ethnicity and socioeconomic class overlap in ways that extend, deepen and entrench exclusion. The author makes a case for the production of ‘counterpublics’ and the role of art in prodding and sustaining alternative understandings of harm and exclusion, as well as an important perspective on how the vandalizing of memorials contributes to contested memory in postconflict sites. Here active memory and art as a justice-oriented political practice fuse method and substance together. The ecology of marginalization is dense. Two articles bring a highly underrepresented group into sharper focus, namely children who are the offspring of conflict, shaped by conflict, and who bear the intergenerational legacies of exposure and parental trauma concurrently with their own. Tatiana Sanchez Parra writes of children born during the war in Colombia, the product of rape and sexual violence. Without sensationalizing and without seeking to detract from the harms experienced by their birth mothers, the article gives independent voice to the autonomous facets of their lives. Their social navigation in a postwar political community, and the tensions that lie in highlighting their lives or ignoring their existence as a political matter are explored through the well-trodden transitional justice tools of recognition and acknowledgement. Children embody multiple intersectional identities (age, gender, race, ethnicity, disability) but are all too often lost in the one-dimensional capture of ‘womenandchildren.’ The author’s ethnographic fieldwork gives authentic voice to some of these underrepresented experiences. title: Agentic Leave and Dispatch Automation for Trucking Fleets Using MCP and LLMs
abstract: Large trucking companies employing thousands of drivers operate in a complex work pattern with weekend and night shift operations. These kinds of large fleets face operational disruptions due to unplanned absences by the drivers. Looking up the leave balances in the HR system manually and rescheduling dispatches are slow, error-prone, and often result in unexpected payroll deductions due to insufficient leave balances. This paper presents Conversational Dispatcher Bot installed as an app on mobile phone which leverages Large Language Models (LLM) to understand driver queries and use Model Context Protocol(MCP) for secure enterprise tool calling. Using MCP server bot connects to HR system to check leave balances, leave eligibility, estimates the payroll deductions, process the leave and connects to Scheduling system to reassign affected pickups/drop-offs to the alternate qualified drivers. The proposed architecture transforms driver’s phone into operational control interface reducing the dispatcher workload immensely, improving scheduling continuity, increasing policy transparency and lowering driver attrition through fair and explainable decision-making.

title: LATTE-MV: Learning to Anticipate Table Tennis Hits from Monocular Videos
abstract: Physical agility is a necessary skill in competitive table tennis, but by no means sufficient. Champions excel in this fast-paced and highly dynamic environment by anticipating their opponent's intent - buying themselves the necessary time to react. In this work, we take one step towards designing such an anticipatory agent. Previous works have developed systems capable of real-time table tennis gameplay, though they often do not leverage anticipation. Among the works that forecast opponent actions, their approaches are limited by dataset size and variety. Our paper contributes (1) a scalable system for reconstructing monocular video of table tennis matches in 3D and (2) an uncertainty-aware controller that anticipates opponent actions. We demonstrate in simulation that our policy improves the ball return rate against high-speed hits from 49.9% to 59.0% as compared to a baseline non-anticipatory policy.

title: An approach to designing security model for mobile agent based systems
abstract: This paper considers the design of a security model for mobile agent based computing systems. The security model proposes the notion of a security enhanced agent that captures a variety of security information needed in the provision of security services. It defines the privileges of the agent required to perform the actions, the rights that other principals can have over the agent as well as delegation of privileges. The security model identifies security management and policy based components in agent enabled hosts which interpret the privileges and rights of agents and enforce the security controls.

title: CAPO: Critic-Guided Action-Aligned Policy Optimization for Advancing LLM Agent Capabilities
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a key technique for improving the agentic capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Although critic-free methods such as GRPO are increasingly popular, we argue that critic-based methods remain well suited to long-horizon agentic tasks because their critic models can assess each state and assign credit to different decisions. However, representative critic-based methods such as PPO still organize value estimation, credit assignment, and policy updates at token granularity, whereas the environment state changes only after the agent completes a full action. In this work, we propose CAPO, a critic-guided action-aligned policy optimization method for advancing LLM agent capabilities. CAPO introduces two action-aligned designs. First, it estimates the state value at the action boundary using a critic model and assigns the corresponding advantage to the complete action rather than individual tokens. Second, CAPO introduces a novel action-aware policy ratio that aggregates token ratios within each action with length calibration for consistent updates across actions of different lengths. These two designs effectively achieve fine-grained credit assignment and consistent policy updates while remaining compatible with token-level gradient computation. Experiments across multi-hop QA, academic paper search, and text-world action tasks show that CAPO consistently outperforms representative RL methods. Further analyses validate both designs and reveal how action-aligned optimization improves multi-turn RL training. We hope this work provides a practical path for training more capable LLM agents.
